title: Acute Liver Failure: Recognition, Stabilisation and Transplant-Centre Referral

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acute liver failure (ALF) in the emergency department (ED) or intensive care unit (ICU): definition, cause work-up, severity markers, early contact with a liver transplant centre, King's College and Clichy criteria, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), airway, glucose, sodium, coagulation, infection, circulatory and renal support. Uses the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) 2017 guideline summary and the acetylcysteine product information. Acute-on-chronic liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis are separate topics.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-22.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi ALF guideline was found.
Only the official EASL slide summary was opened, not the full article; locators refer to named sections of the slide summary, not pages.
EASL recommends NAC early in non-paracetamol ALF but the summary gives no dose; the paracetamol regimen from the product information is shown and needs hepatology confirmation.
EASL gives no mean arterial pressure target and no hypertonic saline sodium target beyond correcting sodium to 140 to 150 mmol/L.
Typical normal ranges for INR, ammonia, lactate, bilirubin and creatinine are not from EASL; local laboratory ranges apply.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: ALF is a rare syndrome of acute liver injury with coagulopathy (INR above 1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without prior cirrhosis (EASL ALF 2017, Section Definition and clinical course). It is classed by the interval from jaundice to encephalopathy as hyperacute, acute or subacute (up to 12 weeks) (EASL ALF 2017, Section Definition and clinical course). Raised arterial ammonia, especially above 150 to 200 µmol/L that does not fall, signals risk of cerebral oedema and intracranial hypertension (EASL ALF 2017, Section Intracranial hypertension). Patients are prone to hypoglycaemia, infection, circulatory failure and acute kidney injury (EASL ALF 2017, Sections on glucose, infection, circulation and renal support).

symptoms: Jaundice followed by confusion or drowsiness (EASL ALF 2017, Section Definition and clinical course).
Recent paracetamol, other drug, herbal or toxin exposure (EASL ALF 2017, Section Initial investigations).
Symptoms of viral hepatitis (EASL ALF 2017, Section Initial investigations).
physicalSigns: Hepatic encephalopathy of any grade, which is essential for the diagnosis (EASL ALF 2017, Section Definition and clinical course).
Jaundice (EASL ALF 2017, Section Definition and clinical course).
Hypotension and signs of systemic inflammatory response (EASL ALF 2017, Sections on circulation and infection).
Reduced urine output (EASL ALF 2017, Section Initial investigations).
redFlags: INR above 1.5 with any encephalopathy or other poor prognostic features: transfer early to a specialist liver unit (EASL ALF 2017, Section Transfer).
Encephalopathy grade 3 to 4: intubate to protect the airway (EASL ALF 2017, Section Encephalopathy).
Arterial ammonia above 150 to 200 µmol/L not falling with treatment: high risk of intracranial hypertension (EASL ALF 2017, Section Intracranial hypertension).
Hypoglycaemia, which is common and linked to higher mortality (EASL ALF 2017, Section Glucose).
King's College or Clichy criteria met: transplant listing discussion (EASL ALF 2017, Section Prognostic criteria).
precipitants: Paracetamol overdose (EASL ALF 2017, Section Prognostic criteria).
Other drug-induced liver injury (EASL ALF 2017, Section Prognostic criteria).
Hepatitis A, B, E, herpes simplex, varicella zoster, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus and parvovirus (EASL ALF 2017, Section Initial investigations).
Autoimmune hepatitis (EASL ALF 2017, Section Initial investigations).

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise ALF and send the admission panel
actions: Confirm coagulopathy and encephalopathy and exclude chronic liver disease (EASL ALF 2017, Section Definition and clinical course).

Send coagulation, liver, renal, blood gas, lactate, ammonia, lipase, paracetamol level, toxicology, viral and autoimmune tests, cultures, chest X-ray, ECG and liver ultrasound (EASL ALF 2017, Section Initial investigations).

clinicalManagement.title: Call the transplant centre early
actions: Transfer early to a specialised unit when INR is above 1.5 with encephalopathy or other poor prognostic features; possible contraindications to transplant should not delay transfer (EASL ALF 2017, Section Transfer).
Apply King's College and Clichy criteria with the transplant team (EASL ALF 2017, Section Prognostic criteria).

clinicalManagement.title: Start NAC
actions: Give NAC early when coagulopathy and raised aminotransferases are present, including non-paracetamol cases (see Medicines) (EASL ALF 2017, Section Specific management).

clinicalManagement.title: Protect the brain and airway
actions: Avoid sedatives as a preventive measure (EASL ALF 2017, Section Encephalopathy).
Grade 3 to 4 encephalopathy: intubate; in grade 4 target arterial carbon dioxide 4.5 to 5.5 kPa, sedate with propofol and use a short-acting opioid (EASL ALF 2017, Section Encephalopathy).
Correct hyponatraemia to 140 to 150 mmol/L (EASL ALF 2017, Section Intracranial hypertension).

clinicalManagement.title: Organ support
actions: Check glucose often and correct hypoglycaemia without causing hyperglycaemia (EASL ALF 2017, Section Glucose).
Do not give fresh frozen plasma or coagulation factors routinely; use them for procedures such as intracranial pressure monitor insertion or active bleeding (EASL ALF 2017, Section Coagulation).
Take surveillance cultures; start antibiotics if encephalopathy progresses, infection is suspected or systemic inflammatory response appears (EASL ALF 2017, Section Infection).
Use noradrenaline as first-choice vasopressor (EASL ALF 2017, Section Circulation).
Use continuous rather than intermittent renal replacement therapy (EASL ALF 2017, Section Renal support).
Give enteral or parenteral nutrition; avoid nasogastric feeding in progressing encephalopathy (EASL ALF 2017, Section Nutrition).

regimens.indication: Paracetamol-related acute liver injury or failure
regimens.dose: Bag 1: 150 mg/kg in 200 mL over 1 hour; Bag 2: 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 hours; Bag 3: 100 mg/kg in 1 litre over 16 hours; total 300 mg/kg over 21 hours, in glucose 5% preferably (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.2). PAEDIATRIC: same mg/kg doses with smaller volumes (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.2).
regimens.frequency: Three consecutive infusions without a break
regimens.duration: 21 hours; continue at the bag 3 rate if liver injury persists (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.2)
adjustments: Use actual body weight, capped at 110 kg (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.2).
Children: same mg/kg doses with fluid volumes reduced for weight; for 12 kg, 38 mL, 100 mL and 200 mL for the three bags (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.2).
Under 40 kg, fluid restriction or children: risk of fluid overload, hyponatraemia and seizures (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.4).
No renal or hepatic dose change is stated in the SmPC.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Watch for anaphylactoid reactions, mostly during the loading bag; pause the infusion, treat, then restart at a lower rate (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Sections 4.4 and 4.8).
Plasma potassium and electrocardiogram (ECG) (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.8).
International normalised ratio (INR), liver tests and creatinine to decide whether to continue the third-bag rate (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.2).
contraindications: No contraindication in paracetamol overdose (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.3).
Higher risk of anaphylactoid reaction with asthma or atopy (Acetylcysteine SmPC, Section 4.4).

medicationPlan.note: NAC is the only drug listed. The 21-hour regimen is the paracetamol overdose regimen; EASL supports NAC in early non-paracetamol ALF without giving a dose. Antibiotics follow the local ICU protocol. diagnosticCriteria.threshold: INR above 1.5 or prolonged prothrombin time with hepatic encephalopathy, no pre-existing cirrhosis, illness up to 12 weeks (EASL ALF 2017, Section Definition and clinical course).

Arterial pH below 7.3 after resuscitation and more than 24 hours after ingestion; or lactate above 3 mmol/L; or all of encephalopathy above grade 3, creatinine above 300 µmol/L and INR above 6.5 (EASL ALF 2017, Section Prognostic criteria).

INR above 6.5; or 3 of 5: indeterminate or drug aetiology, age under 10 or over 40, jaundice-to-encephalopathy over 7 days, bilirubin above 300 µmol/L, INR above 3.5 (EASL ALF 2017, Section Prognostic criteria).
Grade 3 to 4 encephalopathy with factor V below 20% under 30 years, or below 30% at 30 years or more (EASL ALF 2017, Section Prognostic criteria).

teaching.scope: Adults with acute liver failure (ALF) in the emergency department (ED) or intensive care unit (ICU): definition, cause work-up, severity markers, early contact with a liver transplant centre, King's College and Clichy criteria, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), airway, glucose, sodium, coagulation, infection, circulatory and renal support. Uses the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) 2017 guideline summary and the acetylcysteine product information. Acute-on-chronic liver failure and hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis are separate topics.
learningObjectives: Define ALF and separate it from chronic liver disease.
Send the cause and severity panel.
Contact the transplant centre early and know King's College and Clichy criteria.
Start NAC and support organs safely.
pitfalls: Delaying transfer until criteria for transplant are met.
Giving fresh frozen plasma without a procedure or bleeding.
keyPoints: Encephalopathy is required for the diagnosis.
INR above 1.5 with encephalopathy means early transfer.
Do not correct INR with plasma routinely; it is a prognostic marker.

patientEducation: Your liver has suddenly stopped working well; you need specialist liver care, which may include a transplant.
Family should tell staff about all medicines, herbal products and paracetamol taken.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid alcohol and any unprescribed medicine or herbal product after recovery.
Nutrition support as advised by the dietitian (EASL ALF 2017, Section Nutrition).
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; hepatologist; ICU; liver transplant centre; toxicology or poisons service; dietitian; psychiatry after deliberate overdose.
dischargeCriteria: Encephalopathy resolved, INR and liver tests improving, eating, cause identified and treated, psychiatric review after overdose, hepatology follow-up booked.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Hepatology follow-up of liver tests and cause-specific treatment; transplant centre follow-up after transplant (EASL ALF 2017, Section Transfer).
